forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Staffordshire forecasts an £8.896m overspend for 2026/27, with Children in Care £16.9m over budget
news_drafts.lead:
Staffordshire County Council is forecasting a net overspend of £8.896m on its day-to-day running costs (revenue spending) for 2026/27. A forecast overspend is where a council expects to end the year having spent more than it budgeted. The quarter 2 performance report, due before the Corporate Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 27 October, puts the forecast outturn, the expected actual figure for the year, at £805.684m against a revised budget of £796.787m. That is an overspend of 1.12%.

Children in Care is forecast at £132.323m for the year against a revised budget of £115.423m, an overspend of £16.9m. The revenue forecast paper shows it as the largest single line variance and the main part of the overspend in Children and Families. It says the overspend comes from portfolio budgets, partly offset by centrally controlled items. The performance report attributes the pressure in Families & Communities to increased demand and higher costs for Children in Care, particularly residential placements.

The report says "an in-year cost recovery plan is in place to help reduce the impact". It also says work is under way to strengthen in-house provision and to secure placements that offer value for money. The papers give no figure for what the plan is expected to recover.

news_drafts.headline: Staffordshire forecasts £8.896m overspend for 2026-27, with children in care costs £16.9m over budget
news_drafts.lead:
Staffordshire County Council is forecasting that it will spend £8.896m more than its budget this year, according to the quarter 2 performance report going to Cabinet on 21 October. The forecast outturn (the expected full-year spending) is £805.684m, against a revised budget of £796.787m, an overspend of 1.12%.

The report says the overspend is largely due to Families and Communities, where there is "exceptional pressure from the increased demand and cost for Children in Care, especially where there is a requirement for residential placements". Within the Children and Families portfolio, children in care is forecast to spend £132.323m against a budget of £115.423m, a difference of £16.9m. Family Help and Safeguarding is forecast £4.6m over. The portfolio as a whole is forecast to overspend by £18.6m. The report says 1,431 children were in care in August, a rate of 82.8 per 10,000, and describes that rate as "high".

The council says work is under way "to strengthen in-house provision, secure high-quality placements that offer value for money, and implement a cost recovery plan to help reduce the impact of these pressures". The papers give no target for how much the plan will reduce the overspend, and no timetable.

news_drafts.headline: Staffordshire schools-funding deficit rose from £53.6m to £94.4m in a year; override ends March 2028
news_drafts.lead:
Staffordshire County Council's deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) reached £94.4m in March 2026, up from £53.6m a year earlier, an increase of £40.8m. The figure appears in the draft value for money opinion for 2025/26, the external auditor's view on whether the council manages its money and decisions properly, which went to the Audit and Standards Committee on 29 September.

The paper says the statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, "will remain in place to 31 March 2028". Councils "will need to plan to meet the cost of any residual deficits from their own reserves in 2028-29", it states. The paper also describes a temporary government High Needs Stability Grant, covering up to 90%, which depends on approval of the council's plan for reforming support for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

The committee also received an internal audit progress update. Of 36 high-priority recommendations in corporate areas, one was overdue at 16 September 2026. It concerns the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special needs. The recommendation, due 31 July 2026, asked the council to review its debt position on that block and set clear arrangements for reporting and managing the risks. The update records no progress from management.

findings.headline: Capital maintenance programme delivers 99.7% of planned works
findings.detail: The paper says the capital maintenance delivery programme is on track, with 99.7% of planned works delivered and major schemes completed, including Derby Road Phase 3 in Burton upon Trent and Lodge Lane roundabout in Saredon.
findings.matters: Delivering almost all planned capital maintenance works in-year is evidence of programme control, which finance directors compare against slippage elsewhere in their own capital programmes.
findings.quote: Capital maintenance delivery programme status remains on track, with 99.7% of planned works delivered

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation activity is paused pending the Government's review
findings.detail: The paper says LGR activity is paused pending the Government's review, but the Council continues preparing for devolution, with programme governance, delivery planning and stakeholder engagement under way.
findings.matters: Councils in reorganisation or devolution processes need to know whether their financial planning assumptions and transition budgets will still hold once the review concludes.
findings.quote: While Local Government Reorganisation activity is currently paused pending the Government’s review

findings.headline: New small format advertising contract awarded, with digital bus information totems being installed
findings.detail: The paper reports four digital bus information totems being installed and more locations going through planning. It says a new small format advertising contract has been awarded and implementation is under way.
findings.matters: Advertising is a commercial income line councils are increasingly using to offset budget pressure, and finance directors may compare contract terms and income expectations.
findings.figures: Four digital bus information totems being installed
findings.quote: A new small format advertising contract has also been awarded, with implementation now underway.

findings.headline: Night-Time Economy Strategy consideration moves from July to October 2026
findings.detail: The paper says development of the Night-Time Economy Strategy has been delayed by around three months, with consideration moving from July to October 2026 to allow further work on options. It states the revised timetable remains on track.
findings.matters: A slipped strategy deadline is a delivery signal that peers planning similar strategies will compare against their own timetables.
findings.figures: Around three months' delay; July to October 2026
findings.quote: Development of the Night-Time Economy Strategy has been delayed by around three months

findings.headline: Cabinet approves £28.6m of government grant for a special school in Rugeley and a primary Pupil Referral Unit in Stafford
findings.detail: The paper says Cabinet approved £28.6m of government grant funding in July for a new special school in Rugeley and a primary Pupil Referral Unit in Stafford. The schemes form part of the expansion of specialist provision.
findings.matters: Using a specific government grant to fund new special school capacity is the kind of SEND capital decision finance directors and lenders watch as high-needs demand grows.
findings.quote: In July, Cabinet approved £28.6m of government grant funding for a new special school in Rugeley
